chunks: If I take two inverting gates and cross-couple them, like two NOR gates where each output feeds the other's input, I get a circuit with two stable states, so it remembers one bit.
That's the SR latch: pulse S to set the output high, pulse R to reset it low, and with both low it holds.
The one forbidden case is both inputs high, which forces both outputs to the same value and gives unpredictable behavior when you release them.
To make it more useful, I add gating. A gated D latch has a data input D and an enable. When enable is high, D controls the latch, so Q follows D, so it's transparent.
When enable is low, the inputs are blocked and the loop just holds. D can only produce set or reset, so the forbidden state is gone.
A flip-flop is two D latches in series with opposite enables. When the clock is low, the first one, the master, is transparent and the second is holding.
At the rising edge the master closes and keeps the value D had at that moment, and the second one, the slave, opens and passes it to the output.
So the output changes only at the clock edge.

Physically, the master's setup and hold times come from how long it takes the master loop to settle before it closes, and metastability is what happens if D changes at that moment and the loop is left balanced at the unstable midpoint."
